one_liner: Seastar thread-per-core O_DIRECT write-ahead log from the smf project; ~48x lower worst-case produce latency than Kafka 1.0.
what_it_does: A sharded, append-only topic/partition log (write_ahead_log::append/get taking Flatbuffers requests and returning Seastar futures), fronted by the smfb broker, which accepted batched puts over smf RPC. It was removed from smf master on 2018-02-24 (commit 6addb463cc, issue #203), 16 days after the benchmark post. The repo is now only the smf RPC framework, so the WAL exists only in git history (last at commit 772474eb02). It has a different interface from Kafka: no Kafka wire protocol, no consumer API, and the broker's get() handler returns status 500 unconditionally.
how_it_is_fast: It uses Seastar shard-per-core ownership. Each topic/partition is routed to one core by jump consistent hash and has a single reader/writer, with no locks or atomics. Writes are copied into page-aligned 4 KB chunks and sent as O_DIRECT dma_write calls (up to 4 concurrent per segment) once 1 MB is pending or a flush timer fires, with segments rolled at 64 MB and tagged with Seastar IO priority classes. The 48x result came from a perf/toplev pass: removing a per-put std::sort (74% of CPU), replacing a map.find with std::lower_bound over a std::deque (offsets are monotonic), and caching each entry's on-disk size to cut LLC misses.
when_to_use: You are building a Seastar service and want a reference O_DIRECT segment writer with page-aligned chunking, bounded concurrent DMA writes, and a size-or-time flush policy to port.
Write-heavy ingest of small records (about 100 B) in large client batches, where acknowledging after in-memory buffering (log-writer semantics, as the author concedes) is acceptable.
Single-node, per-core-partitioned append logs on Linux + XFS + NVMe, where you can pin cores and route each partition to its owning shard.
Studying a documented profiling case (perf record/stat, toplev, LLC-miss hunting) on a real log-write path.
when_not_to_use: As a Kafka replacement. It has no Kafka protocol, no replication (chain_replication_service::put only appends locally), no consumer groups, and broker-side reads return 500. The reader code has an in-progress 'XXX working on this' path.
When you need per-write durability. The write path has no fdatasync, the timer flush defaults to 1 minute (smfb used the default), and acks return before DMA writes finish.

When you want a maintained dependency. It was deleted from master in Feb 2018, is written against the 2018 Seastar API (old <core/...> include paths), and was built with an Ansible-provisioned Seastar, so expect a port before it compiles.
Non-Linux, non-x86 or small hosts. smfb refuses to start without SSE4.2, throws below 1 GiB of memory per shard unless --developer is set, and logs an error when the log directory is not on XFS.

integration.dependencies: Seastar (early-2018, with libaio; DPDK optional), Flatbuffers, Boost, zstd, lz4, xxHash, RE2, Roaring bitmaps, HdrHistogram; smf RPC for the smfb broker
integration.min_toolchain: GCC with Seastar-era flags (CMake enables -fconcepts for GCC > 6.1); CMake 3.3+; C++ standard inherited from Seastar pkg-config flags, not stated
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 with SSE4.2 (broker check); XFS expected; O_DIRECT/AIO required
integration.thread_safety: Seastar sharded<T>: each core owns its partitions, and requests must be submitted on the owning core (a wrong-core append throws in debug builds). There is no cross-thread locking.

gotchas: In wal_segment, append() and do_flush() launch dma_write in the background without awaiting it (commented 'send in background - safely!!'). As written, flush() and close() do not wait for in-flight writes, and write errors are not propagated to the ack.
wal_segment::open() throws if the segment file already exists, and files are opened with create|truncate. Recovery and reopen depend on epoch-named new files, not on appending to old ones.
Partition routing is the caller's job (jump_consistent_hash(partition, smp::count)). Misrouting shows up as directory or system_error failures, per the header comment.

The headline numbers disagree across the author's own sources: the blog says 48x (max latency only), the deleted docs page says 34-43x across percentiles, commit 5585e52f45 says '4x faster than kafka to 91X', and issue #195 says '10x lower latency'.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Redpanda (a maintained, Kafka-API-compatible C++ broker also built on Seastar) for any production Kafka replacement, and Walrus (maintained Rust log engine) when you need an embeddable log. Pick the SMF WAL only as a small, Apache-2.0 reference design for a Seastar-native O_DIRECT log writer that you will port and harden yourself.
verified_claims_summary: On one localhost Linux 4.14 host (NVMe + XFS; CPU and compiler version not stated; release builds of that era used -O2 -ggdb per CMake/base_flags.cmake), using Seastar epoll + AIO without DPDK, smfb's slowest write took 34 ms versus 1618 ms for Kafka 1.0.0's ProducerPerformance (100M 100-byte records, acks=1, lz4, 32 partitions). That is about 48x on maximum latency only, with no percentile table or throughput. An earlier, since-deleted docs page (2 bare-metal dual Xeon E5-2640 v3 servers, SATA SSD, DPDK server, Kafka 0.11.0.1) reported 34-43x lower latency percentiles and 1.71M vs 0.42M msgs/s with 1 producer, or 2.27M vs 0.96M with 3 producers.
status_note: Abandoned: the WAL was deleted from master in Feb 2018, and the repo (last master commit 2021-10-17) is now RPC-only. The Apache-2.0 code can be recovered from commit 772474eb02, but it is tied to a 2018 Seastar API and has unfinished reads and weak durability, so treat it as reference code, not a dependency.
